title: An architect cracked a script that had stumped scholars for 50 years
body: Linear B, found on clay tablets at Knossos in Crete and on the Greek mainland, was written in the Bronze Age, centuries before the Greek alphabet. In 1952 Michael Ventris, a young English architect working in his spare time, showed that its language was an early form of Greek. That pushed written Greek back to around 1450 BC, though its older cousin, Linear A, remains undeciphered.

slides.heading: A promise at 14
slides.text: As a schoolboy in 1936, Michael Ventris, later an architect, heard archaeologist Arthur Evans talk about the mysterious Linear B tablets of Knossos and resolved to decipher them.

slides.heading: Kober’s groundwork
slides.text: American scholar Alice Kober spotted words whose endings changed like grammatical inflections. Her analysis laid the foundations Ventris built on.

slides.heading: The place-name hunch
slides.text: Some sign groups appeared only on tablets from Crete. Ventris guessed they were Cretan towns such as Knossos, and the sound values fell into place.

slides.heading: The tripod test
slides.text: In 1953 a tablet from Pylos showed a drawing of a tripod cauldron beside signs reading ti-ri-po-de, Greek for tripods. Ventris had originally expected Etruscan.

slides.heading: Which script is still undeciphered?
slides.explanation: Ventris read Linear B as Greek in 1952, and hieroglyphs and cuneiform were cracked in the 19th century. Linear A, Linear B’s older cousin, remains unread.

slides.question: Which language did Ventris originally expect Linear B to hide?
slides.explanation: Ventris had expected Etruscan. His place-name hunch showed the language was an early form of Greek, and the 1953 tripod tablet from Pylos confirmed it.
